patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Carmen Herrera is a 54-year-old right-handed woman and IT project manager who presents with a two-month history of progressive difficulty finding words during her lectures, accompanied by subtle personality changes noticed primarily by her husband. Her husband reports that approximately two months ago, she began pausing more frequently during dinner conversations, searching for words that would normally come easily to her. As an English teacher known for her articulate speech and literary references, these pauses were immediately noticeable to her family and eventually to her colleagues. Over the past month, the word-finding difficulty has worsened, and she has started using circumlocutions — describing objects rather than naming them. Her husband also reports that she has become unusually irritable and short-tempered over the past six weeks, which is quite unlike her typically patient demeanor. She has had two episodes of unprovoked crying at work, leading to embarrassment and contributing to her decision to take medical leave one week ago. She describes a dull, persistent left-sided headache that developed approximately three weeks ago, which she initially attributed to stress and treated with ibuprofen. Unlike her typical migraines, this headache is constant rather than episodic, is not associated with photophobia or phonophobia, and only partially responds to her usual analgesics. She denies any nausea or vomiting. She has also noticed increasing fatigue and difficulty concentrating while grading papers, tasks she previously managed with ease. There has been no witnessed seizure activity, no episodes of loss of consciousness, and no visual disturbances that she has recognized, although her husband noted she has been bumping into doorframes on her right side more frequently over the past two weeks. She denies any fevers, weight loss, night sweats, or new skin lesions. She has no history of cancer and no known exposures to carcinogens. Her primary care physician initially attributed her symptoms to depression and work-related burnout, but after failing to improve on a short trial of sertraline and given the progressive nature of her symptoms, he ordered a brain MRI which revealed a left temporal lesion, prompting urgent referral and admission.
